title: Manual Cache Invalidation Techniques
description: Learn how to programmatically remove or update cache entries when data changes outside of TTL expiration.

data.text: TTL-based expiration is automatic and simple, but it is not enough when data changes unpredictably. If a user updates their profile, a product price changes, or an admin publishes new content, waiting for the TTL to run out means serving stale data. **Manual invalidation** gives your application direct control over when cached entries are removed or refreshed.
Manual invalidation is the backbone of cache consistency in write-heavy or real-time applications. It keeps the cache aligned with the database without relying solely on time-based expiration.

terms.definition: The process of removing or updating a cached entry because the underlying data has changed.
A strategy that writes to both the cache and the database simultaneously so the cache is always up to date.
A strategy that writes to the cache first and persists to the database asynchronously.
A strategy that updates the database first and then removes or updates the related cache entry.

data.text: Redis provides several commands for removing cache entries. `DEL` removes one or more keys by name. `UNLINK` is an asynchronous variant that frees memory in the background. `FLUSHDB` and `FLUSHALL` wipe entire databases or all databases, respectively — useful in development but dangerous in production.

data.title: Redis — Manual invalidation commands
data.content: Remove a specific cached product, then remove all cached categories.
data.code:
# Remove a single key
DEL product:42:details

# Asynchronous removal (non-blocking)
UNLINK product:42:details product:43:details

# Remove all keys matching a pattern
redis-cli --scan --pattern 'category:*' | xargs redis-cli DEL

data.text: In a typical web application, you invalidate the cache immediately after a successful database write. The exact placement depends on your architecture: a repository method, a service-layer event handler, or a domain-event subscriber.

cards.title: Write-Through
cards.description: Write to cache and database in the same transaction.

cards.title: Write-Invalidate
cards.description: Write to database first, then delete the cache entry.

cards.title: Write-Behind
cards.description: Write to cache immediately, flush to database asynchronously.

data.title: Invalidate related keys too
data.text: A single database row may appear in multiple cache keys — user lists, search results, aggregated dashboards. Invalidation must account for all derived keys, or you will serve stale aggregated data even after the source is updated.

data.caption: Write-invalidate flow: the database is updated first, then the related cache entries are removed so the next read rebuilds them.
data.definition:
graph LR
    A[Client Update] --> B[Write to Database]
    B --> C[Delete Cache Key]
    C --> D[Next Read]
    D --> E[Cache Miss]
    E --> F[Read from Database]
    F --> G[Write to Cache]
    G --> H[Return Fresh Value]

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Use DEL or UNLINK to remove specific keys programmatically.
Invalidate cache entries immediately after successful database writes.
Consider all derived cache keys when invalidating aggregated or list data.
Write-invalidate is a safe default for most applications.
data.takeaway: Manual invalidation keeps the cache honest — remove stale entries the moment the source data changes.
